{{Short description|Exact spherically symmetric solution in GR}}
{{general relativity sidebar}}
In [[general relativity]], the '''Vaidya metric''' describes the non-empty external spacetime of a spherically symmetric and nonrotating star which is either emitting or absorbing [[Null dust solution|null dusts]]. It is named after the Indian physicist [[Prahalad Chunnilal Vaidya]] and constitutes the simplest non-static generalization of the non-radiative [[Schwarzschild metric|Schwarzschild solution]] to [[Einstein's field equation]], and therefore is also called the "radiating(shining) Schwarzschild metric".

== From Schwarzschild to Vaidya metrics ==

The Schwarzschild metric as the static and spherically symmetric solution to Einstein's equation reads
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> ds^2=-\left( 1-\frac{2M}{r} \right) dt^2 + \left( 1-\frac{2M}{r} \right)^{-1}dr^2+r^2 \left(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right).</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

To remove the coordinate singularity of this metric at <math>r=2M</math>, one could switch to the [[Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates]]. Thus, introduce the "retarded(/outgoing)" null coordinate <math>u</math> by
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> t=u+r+2M\ln\left(\frac{r}{2M}-1\right)\qquad\Rightarrow\quad dt=du+\left( 1-\frac{2M}{r} \right)^{-1} dr\;,</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}
and Eq(1) could be transformed into the "retarded(/outgoing) Schwarzschild metric"
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> ds^2=-\left( 1-\frac{2M}{r} \right) du^2- 2du dr + r^2\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right);</math>|{{EquationRef|3}}}}
or, we could instead employ the "advanced(/ingoing)" null coordinate <math>v</math> by
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> t=v-r-2M\ln\left(\frac{r}{2M}-1\right)\qquad\Rightarrow\quad dt=dv-\left( 1-\frac{2M}{r} \right)^{-1}dr\;,</math>|{{EquationRef|4}}}}
so Eq(1) becomes the "advanced(/ingoing) Schwarzschild metric"
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> ds^2=-\left( 1-\frac{2M}{r} \right) dv^2+2dvdr+r^2 \left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right).</math>|{{EquationRef|5}}}}

Eq(3) and Eq(5), as static and spherically symmetric solutions, are valid for both ordinary celestial objects with finite radii and singular objects such as [[black holes]]. It turns out that, it is still physically reasonable if one extends the mass parameter <math>M</math> in Eqs(3) and Eq(5) from a constant to functions of the corresponding null coordinate, <math>M(u)</math> and <math>M(v)</math> respectively, thus
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> ds^2 = -\left( 1-\frac{2M(u)}{r} \right) du^2 - 2 du dr + r^2\left(d\theta^2 +\ sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right),</math>|{{EquationRef|6}}}}
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> ds^2=-\left( 1-\frac{2M(v)}{r} \right) dv^2 + 2 dv dr+r^2 \left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right).</math>|{{EquationRef|7}}}}

The extended metrics Eq(6) and Eq(7) are respectively the "retarded(/outgoing)" and "advanced(/ingoing)" Vaidya metrics.<ref name=Vaidya-1>Eric Poisson. ''A Relativist's Toolkit: The Mathematics of Black-Hole Mechanics''. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2004. Section 4.3.5 and Section 5.1.8.</ref><ref name=Vaidya-2>Jeremy Bransom Griffiths, Jiri Podolsky. ''Exact Space-Times in Einstein's General Relativity''. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2009. Section 9.5.</ref> It is also sometimes useful to recast the Vaidya metrics Eqs(6)(7) into the form
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> ds^2 =\frac{2M(u)}{r}du^2 +ds^2(\text{flat})=\frac{2M(v)}{r}dv^2 +ds^2(\text{flat})\,,</math>|{{EquationRef|8}}}}
where <math> ds^2(\text{flat})</math> represents the metric of [[flat spacetime]]: <math display="block">\begin{align}
ds^2(\text{flat}) &= - du^2 - 2 du dr+r^2 \left(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\, d\phi^2 \right) \\
&= - dv^2 +2 dv dr+r^2 \left(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\, d\phi^2 \right) \\
&= -dT^2+dr^2+r^2 \left(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\, d\phi^2 \right)
\end{align}</math>
using <math>T = t - 2M\ln(r/2M-1)</math>.

==Outgoing Vaidya with pure Emitting field==

As for the "retarded(/outgoing)" Vaidya metric Eq(6),<ref name=Vaidya-1/><ref name=Vaidya-2/><ref name=Vaidya-3>Thanu Padmanabhan. ''Gravitation: Foundations and Frontiers''. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2010. Section 7.3.</ref><ref name=Vaidya-4>Pankaj S Joshi. ''Global Aspects in Gravitation and Cosmology''. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996. Section 3.5.</ref><ref name=Vaidya-5>Pankaj S Joshi. ''Gravitational Collapse and Spacetime Singularities''. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2007. Section 2.7.6.</ref> the [[Ricci tensor]] has only one nonzero component
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> R_{uu}=-2\frac{M(u)_{,\,u}}{r^2}\,,</math>|{{EquationRef|9}}}}
while the [[Ricci curvature scalar]] vanishes, <math>R=g^{ab} R_{ab}=0</math> because <math>g^{uu}=0</math>. Thus, according to the trace-free Einstein equation <math>G_{ab}=R_{ab}=8\pi T_{ab}</math>, the [[stress–energy tensor]] <math>T_{ab}</math> satisfies
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> T_{ab}=-\frac{M(u)_{,\,u}}{4\pi r^2} l_a l_b\;,\qquad l_a dx^a=-du\;,</math>|{{EquationRef|10}}}}
where <math>l_a=-\partial_au</math> and <math>l^a=g^{ab}l_b</math> are null (co)vectors (c.f. Box A below). Thus, <math>T_{ab}</math> is a "pure radiation field",<ref name=Vaidya-1/><ref name=Vaidya-2/> which has an energy density of <math display="inline">-\frac{M(u)_{,\,u}}{4\pi r^2}</math>. According to the null [[energy conditions]]
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> T_{ab}k^ak^b\geq 0\;,</math>|{{EquationRef|11}}}}
we have <math>M(u)_{,\,u}<0</math> and thus the central body is emitting radiation.

Following the calculations using [[Newman–Penrose formalism|Newman–Penrose (NP) formalism]] in Box A, the outgoing Vaidya spacetime Eq(6) is of [[Petrov Type|Petrov-type D]], and the nonzero components of the [[Weyl scalar|Weyl-NP]] and [[Ricci scalars (Newman–Penrose formalism)|Ricci-NP]] scalars are
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> \Psi_2=-\frac{M(u)}{r^3}\qquad \Phi_{22}=-\frac{M(u)_{\,,\,u}}{r^2}\;.</math>|{{EquationRef|12}}}}

It is notable that, the Vaidya field is a pure radiation field rather than [[electromagnetic field]]s. The emitted particles or energy-matter flows have zero [[rest mass]] and thus are generally called "null dusts", typically such as photons and [[neutrinos]], but cannot be electromagnetic waves because the Maxwell-NP equations are not satisfied. The outgoing and ingoing null expansion rates for the [[line element]] Eq(6) are respectively
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> \theta_{(\ell)} = -(\rho+\bar\rho) = \frac{2}{r}\,,\quad \theta_{(n)}=\mu+\bar\mu=\frac{-r+2M(u)}{r^2}\;.</math>|{{EquationRef|13}}}}

Suppose <math display="inline">F:=1-\frac{2M(u)}{r} </math>, then the Lagrangian for null radial [[Geodesics in general relativity|geodesics]] <math>(L=0, \dot\theta=0, \dot\phi=0)</math> of the "retarded(/outgoing)" Vaidya spacetime Eq(6) is
<math display="block">L=0=-F\dot{u}^2+2\dot{u}\dot{r}\,,</math>
where dot means derivative with respect to some parameter <math>\lambda</math>. This Lagrangian has two solutions,
<math display="block">\dot{u}=0\quad\text{and}\quad \dot{r} = \frac{F}{2} \dot{u}\;.</math>

According to the definition of <math>u</math> in Eq(2), one could find that when <math>t</math> increases, the areal radius <math>r</math> would increase as well for the solution <math>\dot{u} = 0</math>, while <math>r</math> would decrease for the solution <math display="inline">\dot{r}=\frac{F}{2} \dot{u}</math>. Thus, <math>\dot{u}=0</math> should be recognized as an outgoing solution while <math display="inline">\dot{r} = \frac{F}{2} \dot{u}</math> serves as an ingoing solution. Now, we can [[Construction of a complex null tetrad|construct a complex null tetrad]] which is adapted to the outgoing null radial geodesics and employ the Newman–Penrose formalism for perform a full analysis of the outgoing Vaidya spacetime. Such an outgoing adapted tetrad can be set up as
<math display="block">l^a=(0,1,0,0)\,,\quad n^a=\left(1,-\frac{F}{2},0,0\right)\,,\quad m^a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,r}(0,0,1,i\,\csc\theta)\,,</math>
and the dual basis covectors are therefore
<math display="block">l_a=(-1,0,0,0)\, ,\quad n_a=\left(-\frac{F}{2}, -1,0,0 \right)\,,\quad m_a=\frac{r}{\sqrt{2}}(0,0,1,\sin\theta)\,.</math>

In this null tetrad, the spin coefficients are
<math display="block">\kappa=\sigma=\tau=0\,,\quad \nu=\lambda=\pi=0\,,\quad \varepsilon=0 </math>
<math display="block">\rho=-\frac{1}{r}\,,\quad \mu=\frac{-r+2M(u)}{2r^2}\,,\quad \alpha=-\beta=\frac{-\sqrt{2}\cot\theta}{4r} \,,\quad \gamma=\frac{M(u)}{2r^2}\,.</math>

The [[Weyl scalar|Weyl-NP]] and Ricci-NP scalars are given by
<math display="block">\Psi_0=\Psi_1=\Psi_3=\Psi_4=0\,,\quad \Psi_2=-\frac{M(u)}{r^3}\,,</math>
<math display="block">\Phi_{00} = \Phi_{10} = \Phi_{20} = \Phi_{11} = \Phi_{12} = \Lambda = 0\,,\quad \Phi_{22}=-\frac{M(u)_{\,,\,u}}{r^2}\,,</math>

Since the only nonvanishing Weyl-NP scalar is <math>\Psi_2</math>, the "retarded(/outgoing)" Vaidya spacetime is of Petrov-type D. Also, there exists a radiation field as <math>\Phi_{22}\neq 0</math>.

For the "retarded(/outgoing)" Schwarzschild metric Eq(3), let <math display="inline">G:=1-\frac{2M}{r} </math>, and then the Lagrangian for null radial geodesics will have an outgoing solution <math>\dot{u}=0</math> and an ingoing solution <math display="inline">\dot{r}=-\frac{G}{2}\dot{u}</math>. Similar to Box A, now set up the adapted outgoing tetrad by
<math display="block">l^a=(0,1,0,0)\,,\quad n^a=\left(1,-\frac{G}{2},0,0\right)\,,\quad m^a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,r}(0,0,1,i\,\csc\theta)\,,</math>
<math display="block">l_a=(-1,0,0,0)\, ,\quad n_a=\left(-\frac{G}{2},-1,0,0\right)\,,\quad m_a=\frac{r}{\sqrt{2}}(0,0,1,\sin\theta)\,.</math>
so the spin coefficients are
<math display="block">\kappa=\sigma=\tau=0\,,\quad \nu=\lambda=\pi=0\,,\quad \varepsilon=0 </math>
<math display="block">\rho=-\frac{1}{r}\,,\quad \mu=\frac{-r+2M}{2r^2}\,,\quad \alpha=-\beta=\frac{-\sqrt{2}\cot\theta}{4r}\,,\quad \gamma=\frac{M}{2r^2}\,,</math>
and the Weyl-NP and Ricci-NP scalars are given by
<math display="block">\Psi_0 = \Psi_1 = \Psi_3 = \Psi_4 = 0\,,\quad \Psi_2=-\frac{M}{r^3}\,,</math>
<math display="block">\Phi_{00}=\Phi_{10}=\Phi_{20}=\Phi_{11}=\Phi_{12}=\Phi_{22}=\Lambda=0 \,.</math>

The "retarded(/outgoing)" Schwarzschild spacetime is of Petrov-type D with <math>\Psi_2</math> being the only nonvanishing Weyl-NP scalar.

==Ingoing Vaidya with pure absorbing field==

As for the "advanced/ingoing" Vaidya metric Eq(7),<ref name=Vaidya-1/><ref name=Vaidya-2/><ref name=Vaidya-6>Valeri Pavlovich Frolov, Igor Dmitrievich Novikov. ''Black Hole Physics: Basic Concepts and New Developments''. Berlin: Springer, 1998. Section 5.7.</ref> the Ricci tensors again have one nonzero component
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> R_{vv}=2\frac{M(v)_{,\,v}}{r^2}\,,</math>|{{EquationRef|14}}}}
and therefore <math>R=0</math> and the stress–energy tensor is
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> T_{ab} =\frac{M(v)_{,\,v}}{4\pi r^2}\,n_a n_b \;,\qquad n_a dx^a=-dv\;.</math>|{{EquationRef|15}}}}

This is a pure radiation field with energy density <math display="inline">\frac{M(v)_{,\,v}}{4\pi r^2}</math>, and once again it follows from the null energy condition Eq(11) that <math>M(v)_{,\,v}>0</math>, so the central object is absorbing null dusts. As calculated in Box C, the nonzero Weyl-NP and Ricci-NP components of the "advanced/ingoing" Vaidya metric Eq(7) are
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> \Psi_2=-\frac{M(v)}{r^3}\qquad \Phi_{00}=\frac{M(v)_{\,,\,v}}{r^2}\;.</math>|{{EquationRef|16}}}}

Also, the outgoing and ingoing null expansion rates for the line element Eq(7) are respectively
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> \theta_{(\ell)} = -(\rho+\bar\rho) = \frac{r-2M(v)}{r^2}\,,\quad \theta_{(n)}=\mu+\bar\mu=-\frac{2}{r}\;.</math>|{{EquationRef|17}}}}

The advanced/ingoing Vaidya solution Eq(7) is especially useful in black-hole physics as it is one of the few existing exact dynamical solutions. For example, it is often employed to investigate the differences between different definitions of the dynamical black-hole boundaries, such as the classical [[event horizon]] and the quasilocal trapping horizon; and as shown by Eq(17), the evolutionary hypersurface <math>r=2M(v)</math> is always a marginally outer trapped horizon (<math>\theta_{(\ell)}=0\;, \theta_{(n)}<0</math>).

Suppose <math>\tilde{F}:=1-\frac{2M(v)}{r} </math>, then the Lagrangian for null radial geodesics of the "advanced(/ingoing)" Vaidya spacetime Eq(7) is
<math display="block">L=-\tilde{F}\dot{v}^2+2\dot{v}\dot{r}\,,</math>
which has an ingoing solution <math>\dot{v}=0</math> and an outgoing solution <math display="inline">\dot{r} = \frac{\tilde{F}}{2} \dot{v}</math> in accordance with the definition of <math>v</math> in Eq(4). Now, we can [[Construction of a complex null tetrad|construct a complex null tetrad]] which is adapted to the ingoing null radial geodesics and employ the Newman–Penrose formalism for perform a full analysis of the Vaidya spacetime. Such an ingoing adapted tetrad can be set up as
<math display="block">l^a=\left(1,\frac{\tilde{F}}{2},0,0\right)\,,\quad n^a=(0,-1,0,0)\,,\quad m^a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,r}(0,0,1,i\,\csc\theta)\,,</math>
and the dual basis covectors are therefore
<math display="block">l_a=\left(-\frac{\tilde{F}}{2},1,0,0\right)\,,\quad n_a=(-1,0,0,0)\,,\quad m_a=\frac{r}{\sqrt{2}}(0,0,1,\sin\theta)\,.</math>

In this null tetrad, the spin coefficients are
<math display="block">\kappa=\sigma=\tau=0\,,\quad \nu=\lambda=\pi=0\,,\quad \gamma=0 </math>
<math display="block">\rho=\frac{-r+2M(v)}{2r^2}\,,\quad \mu=-\frac{1}{r}\,,\quad \alpha=-\beta=\frac{-\sqrt{2}\cot\theta}{4r} \,,\quad \varepsilon=\frac{M(v)}{2r^2}\,.</math>

The Weyl-NP and Ricci-NP scalars are given by
<math display="block">\Psi_0=\Psi_1=\Psi_3=\Psi_4=0\,,\quad \Psi_2=-\frac{M(v)}{r^3}\,,</math>
<math display="block">\Phi_{10}=\Phi_{20}=\Phi_{11}=\Phi_{12}=\Phi_{22}=\Lambda=0\,,\quad \Phi_{00}=\frac{M(v)_{\,,\,v}}{r^2}\;.</math>

Since the only nonvanishing Weyl-NP scalar is <math>\Psi_2</math>, the "advanced(/ingoing)" Vaidya spacetime is of [[Petrov Type|Petrov-type D]], and there exists a radiation field encoded into <math>\Phi_{00}</math>.

For the "advanced(/ingoing)" Schwarzschild metric Eq(5), still let <math display="inline">G:=1-\frac{2M}{r} </math>, and then the Lagrangian for the null radial [[Geodesics in general relativity|geodesics]] will have an ingoing solution <math>\dot{v}=0</math> and an outgoing solution <math display="inline">\dot{r} = \frac{G}{2} \dot{v}</math>. Similar to Box C, now set up the adapted ingoing tetrad by
<math display="block">l^a=\left(1,\frac{G}{2},0,0\right)\,,\quad n^a=(0,-1,0,0)\,,\quad m^a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,r}(0,0,1,i\,\csc\theta)\,,</math>
<math display="block">l_a=\left(-\frac{G}{2},1,0,0\right)\,,\quad n_a=(-1,0,0,0)\,,\quad m_a=\frac{r}{\sqrt{2}}(0,0,1,\sin\theta)\,.</math>
so the spin coefficients are
<math display="block">\kappa=\sigma=\tau=0\,,\quad \nu=\lambda=\pi=0\,,\quad \gamma=0 </math>
<math display="block">\rho=\frac{-r+2M}{2r^2}\,,\quad \mu=-\frac{1}{r}\,,\quad \alpha=-\beta=\frac{-\sqrt{2}\cot\theta}{4r} \,,\quad \varepsilon=\frac{M}{2r^2}\,,</math>
and the Weyl-NP and Ricci-NP scalars are given by
<math display="block">\Psi_0=\Psi_1=\Psi_3=\Psi_4=0\,,\quad \Psi_2=-\frac{M}{r^3}\,,</math>
<math display="block">\Phi_{00}=\Phi_{10}=\Phi_{20}=\Phi_{11}=\Phi_{12}=\Phi_{22}=\Lambda=0 \,.</math>

The "advanced(/ingoing)" Schwarzschild spacetime is of Petrov-type D with <math>\Psi_2</math> being the only nonvanishing Weyl-NP scalar.

==Comparison with the Schwarzschild metric==

As a natural and simplest extension of the Schwarzschild metric, the Vaidya metric still has a lot in common with it:

* Both metrics are of Petrov-type D with <math>\Psi_2</math> being the only nonvanishing Weyl-NP scalar (as calculated in Boxes A and B).

However, there are three clear differences between the Schwarzschild and Vaidya metric:

* First of all, the mass parameter <math>M</math> for Schwarzschild is a constant, while for Vaidya <math>M(u)</math> is a u-dependent function.
* Schwarzschild is a solution to the vacuum Einstein equation <math>R_{ab}=0</math>, while Vaidya is a solution to the trace-free Einstein equation <math>R_{ab}=8\pi T_{ab}</math> with a nontrivial pure radiation energy field. As a result, all Ricci-NP scalars for Schwarzschild are vanishing, while we have <math>\Phi_{00}=\frac{M(u)_{\,,\,u}}{r^2}</math> for Vaidya.
* Schwarzschild has 4 independent [[Killing vector field]]s, including a timelike one, and thus is a static metric, while Vaidya has only 3 independent Killing vector fields regarding the spherical symmetry, and consequently is nonstatic. Consequently, the Schwarzschild metric belongs to [[Weyl metrics|Weyl's class of solutions]] while the Vaidya metric does not.

==Extension of the Vaidya metric==

===Kinnersley metric===

While the Vaidya metric is an extension of the Schwarzschild metric to include a pure radiation field, the [[William Morris Kinnersley|Kinnersley metric]]<ref>{{cite journal | last = Kinnersley | first = W. | title=Field of an arbitrarily accelerating point mass | journal=Phys. Rev. | date=October 1969 | volume=186 | issue=5 | page=1335 | doi=10.1103/PhysRev.186.1335 | bibcode = 1969PhRv..186.1335K }}</ref> constitutes a further extension of the Vaidya metric; it describes a massive object that accelerates in recoil as it emits massless radiation anisotropically.
The Kinnersley metric is a special case of the [[Kerr–Schild spacetime|Kerr-Schild metric]], and in cartesian spacetime coordinates <math>x^{\mu}</math> it takes the following form:
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> g_{\mu \nu} = \eta_{\mu \nu} - \frac{2m\bigl(u(x)\bigr)}{r(x)^{3}} \sigma_{\mu}(x) \sigma_{\nu}(x)</math>|{{EquationRef|18}}}}
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> r(x) = \sigma_{\mu}(x) \,\, \lambda^{\mu}(u(x)) </math>|{{EquationRef|19}}}}
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\sigma^{\mu}(x) = X^{\mu}(u(x)) - x^{\mu},
\quad
\eta_{\mu \nu} \sigma^{\mu}(x) \sigma^{\nu}(x) = 0</math>|{{EquationRef|20}}}}
where for the duration of this section all indices shall be raised and lowered using the "flat space" metric <math>\eta_{\mu \nu}</math>, the "mass" <math>m(u)</math> is an arbitrary function of the [[Proper time|proper-time]] <math>u</math> along the mass's [[world line]] as measured using the "flat" metric, <math>du^2 = \eta_{\mu \nu} \, dX^{\mu} dX^{\nu},</math> and <math>X^{\mu}(u)</math> describes the arbitrary world line of the mass, <math>\lambda^{\mu}(u) = dX^{\mu}(u) / du</math> is then the [[four-velocity]] of the mass, <math>\sigma_{\mu}(x)</math> is a "flat metric" null-vector field implicitly defined by Eqn. (20), and <math>u(x)</math> implicitly extends the proper-time parameter to a scalar field throughout spacetime by viewing it as constant on the outgoing light cone of the "flat" metric that emerges from the event <math>X^{\mu}(u),</math> and satisfies the identity <math>\lambda^{\mu}(u(x)) \, \partial_{\mu} u(x) = 1.</math>
Grinding out the [[Einstein tensor]] for the metric <math>g_{\mu \nu}</math> and integrating the outgoing [[energy–momentum tensor|energy–momentum flux]] "at infinity," one finds that the metric <math>g_{\mu \nu}</math> describes a mass
with proper-time dependent [[four-momentum]] <math>P^{\mu} = m(u) \, \lambda^{\mu}(u)</math> that emits a net <<link:0>> at a proper rate of <math>-dP^{\mu}/du;</math> as viewed from the mass's instantaneous rest-frame, the radiation flux has an angular distribution <math>A(u) + B(u) \, \cos(\theta(u)),</math> where <math>A(u)</math> and <math>B(u)</math> are complicated scalar functions of <math>m(u), \lambda^{\mu}(u), \sigma_{\mu}(u),</math> and their derivatives, and <math>\theta(u)</math> is the instantaneous rest-frame angle between the 3-acceleration and the outgoing null-vector.
The Kinnersley metric may therefore be viewed as describing the gravitational field of an accelerating [[photon rocket]] with a very badly collimated exhaust.

In the special case where <math>\lambda^{\mu}</math> is independent of proper-time, the Kinnersley metric reduces to the Vaidya metric.

===Vaidya–Bonner metric===

Since the radiated or absorbed matter might be electrically non-neutral, the outgoing and ingoing Vaidya metrics Eqs(6)(7) can be naturally extended to include varying electric charges,
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> ds^2 = - \left( 1-\frac{2M(u)}{r} + \frac{Q(u)}{r^2} \right) du^2-2dudr+r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)\;,</math>|{{EquationRef|18}}}}
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> ds^2 = -\left( 1-\frac{2M(v)}{r}+\frac{Q(v)}{r^2} \right) dv^2+2dvdr+r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)\;.</math>|{{EquationRef|19}}}}
Eqs(18)(19) are called the Vaidya-Bonner metrics, and apparently, they can also be regarded as extensions of the [[Reissner–Nordström metric]], analogously to the correspondence between Vaidya and Schwarzschild metrics.
